dialect_description: American English is characterized by rhoticity, distinct vowel shifts (such as the Northern Cities Shift and Southern Drawl), and specific vocabulary variations across regions like the Northeast, South, and Midwest.

phonetic_features.description: Pronouncing /t/ or /d/ between vowels as a quick tap.
Replacing /t/ before syllabic /n/ with a glottal catch.
Fully pronouncing the /r/ sound in all positions.
Merging open back vowels (/ɑ/ and /ɒ/) so that 'father' and 'bother' rhyme.

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 90-95% (dominant national language across all states)

dialect_description: Canadian English combines elements of American and British English. Key features include 'Canadian raising' (distinct diphthong pronunciation before voiceless consonants) and the iconic sentence-final particle 'eh'.

phonetic_features.description: Raising the nucleus of diphthongs /aɪ/ and /aʊ/ before voiceless consonants.
Pronouncing vowels in 'cot' and 'caught' identically as an open back unrounded vowel.
Intervocalic /t/ tapping similar to General American.

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 85% (including native speakers and bilingual French-English speakers)

dialect_description: British English features diverse regional accents (e.g., Received Pronunciation, Cockney, Scouse, Geordie, Scottish, Welsh English). It is predominantly non-rhotic and preserves classical spelling and terminology.

phonetic_features.description: Omitting post-vocalic /r/ unless followed by a vowel.
Replacing intervocalic or final /t/ with a glottal stop in casual/accented speech.
Using an open back unrounded vowel in specific short 'a' words.

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 98% (primary native and proficient language)

dialect_description: Guyanese English is heavily influenced by Guyanese Creole (Creolese). Phonetics reflect Caribbean cadence with unique grammatical structures and loanwords from African and Indian languages.

phonetic_features.description: Replacing dental fricatives /θ/ and /ð/ with stops [t] and [d].
Simplifying diphthongs to long pure monophthongs.
Rhythmic stress pattern with consonant cluster reductions.

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 80-90% (English and Creolese used as primary means of communication)

dialect_description: Australian English is famous for extensive use of diminutives and abbreviations ending in '-o' or '-ie', non-rhoticity, flat vowels, and vocabulary influenced by Indigenous Australian languages.

phonetic_features.description: Rising pitch at the end of declarative sentences.
Dropping post-vocalic /r/ sounds completely.
Shifting front vowels towards diphthongized sounds.

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 95% (dominant language across the country)

dialect_description: New Zealand English (NZ English) features distinct vowel shifts (e.g., short 'i' sounds like 'u') and incorporates extensive Māori vocabulary (e.g., 'kia ora', 'whānau').

phonetic_features.description: Pronouncing short /ɪ/ as a schwa sound [ə].
Fronting /ɛ/ sound so that 'pen' sounds like 'pin'.
Standard non-rhotic pronunciation across dialects.

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 96% (primary language of administration and daily life)

dialect_description: Indian English utilizes retroflex consonants, syllable-timed rhythm, unique grammatical forms like continuous tenses with stative verbs, and local idioms directly translated from native languages.

phonetic_features.description: Replacing alveolar plosives /t/ and /d/ with retroflex stops [ʈ] and [ɖ].
Merging fricatives /v/ and /w/ into a single sound.
Giving almost equal duration and stress to each spoken syllable.

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 10-12% (roughly 125-150 million people use English fluently for business, higher education, and administration)

dialect_description: Philippine English is largely modeled after American English but features distinct phonological adaptations, code-switching with Tagalog (Taglish), and unique local vocabulary items.

phonetic_features.description: Substituting /f/ and /v/ with voiceless/voiced plosives [p] and [b].
Merging /ɪ/ and /iː/ vowel sounds.
Not releasing air on word-final voiceless stops [p, t, k].

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 60-70% (widely spoken in business, media, and higher education)

dialect_description: English in PNG is widely influenced by Tok Pisin (an English-based creole). Standard English is used in formal sectors with simplified phonological contrasts.

phonetic_features.description: Simplifying complex vowel systems to a basic 5-vowel inventory (a, e, i, o, u).
Reducing final consonant clusters.
Replacing dental fricatives /θ/ and /ð/ with stops [t] and [d].

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 15-20% (used alongside Tok Pisin in formal and urban sectors)

dialect_description: Nigerian English incorporates tonal influences from indigenous languages like Yoruba, Igbo, and Hausa. Nigerian Pidgin English is also widely spoken informally throughout the country.

phonetic_features.description: Mapping indigenous tonal patterns onto English stress-accent rules.
Eliminating length distinctions between short and long vowels.
Replacing dental fricatives /θ/ and /ð/ with alveolar stops [t] and [d].

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 50-60% (essential lingua franca for inter-ethnic communication, media, and education)

dialect_description: Ghanaian English features syllable-timed intonation, unique idioms reflecting Akan and other local cultural concepts, and reduced vowel distinctions.

phonetic_features.description: Allocating equal timing and weight to unstressed syllables.
Pronouncing diphthongs /eɪ/ and /oʊ/ as pure monophthongs [e] and [o].
Pronouncing /tʃ/ with a soft fricative quality [ʃ].

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 40-50% (widely used in education, administration, and urban areas)

dialect_description: Liberian English is uniquely connected to 19th-century African American Vernacular English (AAVE) alongside local Liberian Kreyol grammar and phonetic influences.

phonetic_features.description: Dropping final consonants or clusters at word endings.
Nasalizing vowels preceding nasal consonants.
Replacing voiced dental fricative /ð/ with voiced stop [d].

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 50-60% (official and standard medium of instruction and government)

dialect_description: Cameroonian English coexists with French and Cameroonian Pidgin English, leading to heavy borrowing, non-rhotic pronunciation, and unique syntactic structures.

phonetic_features.description: Shifting primary stress toward final syllables under French phonological influence.
Neutralizing central vowels /ɜː/ and /ə/ into open front or back vowels.
Simplifying word-final consonant clusters.

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 20-30% (primarily in the Anglophone Northwest and Southwest regions and official sectors)

dialect_description: Sudanese English shows strong phonological influence from Arabic (such as substituting 'p' for 'b') and simplified consonant cluster structures.

phonetic_features.description: Substituting voiceless plosive /p/ with voiced bilabial stop [b].
Inserting an initial vowel to break up starting consonant clusters.
Rolling or trilling the alveolar /r/ sound influenced by Arabic phonology.

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 5-10% (used in higher education, international business, and specific professional circles)

dialect_description: English in South Sudan serves as an official bridging language and shows heavy phonetic influences from East African English and regional Nilo-Saharan languages.

phonetic_features.description: Replacing 'th' sounds [θ] with voiceless dental stops [t].
Merging short and long vowel distinctions.
Strong breath release on initial voiceless stops.

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 10-15% (growing administrative and educational language, alongside Juba Arabic)

dialect_description: Ugandan English ('Uglish') features distinct stress patterns, literal translations from local languages like Luganda, and specific localized colloquialisms.

phonetic_features.description: Interchanging liquid consonants /l/ and /r/.
Shifting stress default to the first syllable of words.
Shifting open back rounded vowels /ɔː/ towards open sounds [a] or [o].

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 30-40% (official language of education, law, and government administration)

dialect_description: Kenyan English exhibits syllable-timed rhythm, vowel reduction shifts influenced by Swahili, and frequent code-mixing known as Sheng in urban settings.

phonetic_features.description: Aligning complex English diphthongs onto a basic 5-vowel Swahili system.
Replacing schwa [ə] with full cardinal vowels.
Replacing dental fricatives /θ/ with alveolar stop [t].

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 30-40% (widely used in commerce, higher education, and official administration)

dialect_description: Tanzanian English is heavily influenced by Swahili phonology, featuring simplified vowel systems and clear syllable-by-syllable pronunciation.

phonetic_features.description: Pronouncing words with equal timing per syllable based on Swahili rhythm.
Inserting explicit full vowels where standard English uses syllabic consonants.
Replacing final /r/ with open vowel endings.

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 15-20% (used in higher education, secondary schools, and international trade)

dialect_description: Malawian English reflects Chichewa phonological rules, with non-rhotic pronunciation, altered vowel lengths, and formal vocabulary derived from British rule.

phonetic_features.description: Substituting /v/ with a voiced bilabial fricative [β].
Merging short /ɪ/ and long /iː/ vowel sounds.
Replacing 'th' sounds with dental stops [t] and [d].

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 25-35% (medium of instruction in secondary/higher education and official governance)

dialect_description: Zambian English displays simplified consonant clusters, pitch intonation influenced by Bemba and Nyanja, and unique localized expressions.

phonetic_features.description: Dropping final consonants in complex blends.
Applying native language tone and pitch accents to English speech.
Simplifying diphthongs /aɪ/ and /aʊ/ into pure single vowels.

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 35-45% (official language of business, media, and education)

dialect_description: Zimbabwean English retains traditional British English grammar alongside distinct Bantu phonetic influences (Shona/Ndebele) and localized idiomatic expressions.

phonetic_features.description: Dropping post-vocalic 'r' sounds in standard register.
Shifting open front vowel /æ/ closer to mid-vowel [e].
Articulating initial /p/, /t/, /k/ without heavy air burst.

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 40-50% (widely used in education, law, media, and government)

dialect_description: Namibian English reflects grammatical and vocabulary influence from Afrikaans and German alongside indigenous languages like Oshiwambo.

phonetic_features.description: Pronouncing consonants with Afrikaans and German guttural traits.
Altering lip rounding on central English vowels.
Pronouncing [t] and [d] with tense tongue positioning.

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 10-15% (administrative and educational language, though Afrikaans and Oshiwambo dominate daily use)

dialect_description: South African English includes unique slang (e.g., 'braai', 'howzit'), non-rhotic pronunciation, and pitch variations influenced by Afrikaans, Zulu, and Xhosa.

phonetic_features.description: Pronouncing short /ɪ/ as [ɪ] in 'kit' but centralizing to [ə] in 'bit'.
Formal articulation of /pʰ/, /tʰ/, /kʰ/ with glottal closure.
Dropping /r/ after vowels entirely.

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 30-35% (major language of commerce, media, politics, and higher education)

english_status: Primary language (native to the majority of the population and state official language alongside Irish)
dialect_description: Hiberno-English (Irish English) is heavily influenced by the Irish Gaelic language (Gaeilge) in syntax, vocabulary, and phonology. It features distinct grammatical structures such as the 'after perfect' tense and a unique melodic intonation.
unique_vocabulary: lads (guys, used for both men and women)
yoke (a thing, object, or gadget whose name is forgotten)

phonetic_features.description: Clear pronunciation of the 'r' sound in all positions (unlike Non-rhotic British English).
Pronouncing dental fricatives (/θ/ and /ð/) as dental stops (/t̪/ and /d̪/), making 'think' sound like 'tink'.
Softening intervocalic or word-final /t/ into a voiceless fricative without closing the vocal tract completely.
Preserving distinct vowel sounds in words that rhyme in other dialects.
phonetic_features.examples: fair vs. fear, horse vs. hoarse

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 98% (virtually universal proficiency alongside Irish)

english_status: Primary language (native to the overwhelming majority of the population and sole official language)
dialect_description: Falkland Islands English (Kelper English) is primarily derived from British West Country and South-East dialects, with noticeable influences from South American Spanish due to historic trade and cattle ranching links. It is non-rhotic or lightly rhotic among younger speakers.
unique_vocabulary: camp (the countryside outside of Stanley, from Spanish 'campo')
camp clean (dressed up neatly for social events in rural areas)
smoko (a short break for tea, coffee, or a cigarette)

phonetic_features.description: Slight or selective pronunciation of post-vocalic /r/, heavily influenced by Southern British English speech patterns.
Retention of Spanish-derived phonetics for rural terminology.

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 99% (primary native and official language)

english_status: Official language (used in government, education, and administration, alongside widespread Belizean Creole and Spanish)
dialect_description: Belizean English is heavily influenced by Belizean Creole (Kriol) and Spanish. Standard Belizean English follows British and American orthographic conventions, while everyday speech blends English vocabulary with Kriol syntax.
unique_vocabulary: cho (an exclamation of surprise, frustration, or annoyance)
panades (deep-fried corn tortillas filled with fish or beans)

phonetic_features.description: Replacing dental fricatives /θ/ and /ð/ with stop consonants /t/ and /d/ in casual speech.
Dropping final /r/ sounds in standard speech under British Caribbean dialect influences.

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 60-70% (official language widely used alongside Belizean Creole and Spanish)

english_status: Official language (Standard Jamaican English used in formal domains; Jamaican Patois/Creole spoken natively by majority)
dialect_description: Jamaican English sits on a post-creole continuum ranging from Standard Jamaican English (similar to Received Pronunciation with Irish and African phonological traits) to Jamaican Patois (Patwa), an English-based creole.
unique_vocabulary: weh yuh ah seh (what are you saying? / how are you?)
small up yuhself (make room / squeeze together)

phonetic_features.description: Omitting initial /h/ in words starting with H, and adding /h/ to words starting with vowels.
Pronouncing /θ/ as /t/ and /ð/ as /d/.
Simplifying diphthongs like /eɪ/ and /oʊ/ into long pure vowels /eː/ and /oː/.

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 95% (Patois and Standard English used across the population)

english_status: Primary and official language (Standard Bahamian English and Bahamian Creole)
dialect_description: Bahamian English shares phonetic features with Gullah and American Southern dialects due to historical migrations of Loyalist settlers and enslaved Africans. Standard speech is formal, while Bahamian Creole is used in everyday informal interactions.
unique_vocabulary: conch (edible sea snail and national dish)
junkanoo (vibrant national festival and street parade)

phonetic_features.description: Interchanging /v/ and /b/ sounds in certain vernacular environments.
Pronouncing dental fricatives as dental stops.

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 98% (primary language of daily life and administration)

english_status: Official language (Standard Trinidadian English; Trinidadian and Tobagonian Creoles spoken daily)
dialect_description: Trinidadian English is characterized by a distinctive musical, sing-song intonation pattern influenced by French Creole (Patois), Spanish, Hindi, and West African languages.
unique_vocabulary: lime (to hang out or socialize with friends)
doubles(popular street food consisting of fried flatbread and curried chickpeas)

phonetic_features.description: Distinctive wide pitch ranges and rhythmic cadence during spoken discourse.
Replacing dental fricatives with alveolar stops.

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 95% (Standard English and Trinidadian Creole universally spoken)

english_status: Co-official language alongside Spanish (extensively used in government, tourism, commerce, and higher education)
dialect_description: Puerto Rican English is influenced by American English due to political association with the United States, as well as Spanish phonology, resulting in code-switching (Spanglish) and rhythmic Spanish-influenced stress patterns.
unique_vocabulary: spanglish (blending of English and Spanish in everyday speech)
parking (car park / parking lot used in local Spanish & English)

phonetic_features.description: Applying Spanish syllable-timed rhythm to spoken English phrases instead of stress-timed rhythm.
phonetic_features.examples: equal duration for unstressed syllables in multisyllabic words

phonetic_features.description: Neutralizing differences between voiced bilabial /b/ and labiodental /v/ sounds.

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 10-20% (fluent bilingual speakers, mostly in professional and tourist sectors alongside Spanish)

english_status: Official language (widely used in government, law, commerce, and higher education)
dialect_description: Pakistani English (PkE) features distinctive local vocabulary, direct translations from Urdu and regional languages, and phonological characteristics shaped by Indo-Aryan languages.

phonetic_features.description: Replacing alveolar /t/ and /d/ with retroflex stops [ʈ] and [ɖ].
Giving equal rhythmic weight and duration to each syllable instead of stress-timing.

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 15-20% (used in higher education, law, high-level governance, and business)

english_status: Official language (used in administration, law, and formal education)
dialect_description: Gambian English is shaped by West African linguistic substrates (such as Mandinka and Wolof) and coexists with Gambian Pidgin English (Criollo) and local languages used in daily life.
unique_vocabulary: tubaab (white person / foreigner, widely used across local English dialogue)

phonetic_features.description: Applying syllable-timed rhythm patterns characteristic of West African languages to English speech.
Replacing dental fricatives /θ/ and /ð/ with alveolar stops [t] and [d].

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 15-25% (used in administration, law, and formal education)

english_status: Official language (used in administration, judiciary, and secondary/higher education)
dialect_description: Sierra Leonean English is heavily influenced by Krio (an English-based creole spoken by over 90% of the population). Standard English is reserved for official settings, while Krio shapes local syntax, idioms, and speech rhythm.

phonetic_features.description: Replacing dental fricatives /θ/ and /ð/ with dental stops [t] and [d].
Adopting the syllable-timed cadence of West African languages and Krio.
phonetic_features.examples: equal stress on syllables in connected speech

phonetic_features.description: Reducing standard diphthongs into monophthongal pure vowels.

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 30-40% (Krio and English serve as widespread mediums in education and urban trade)

english_status: Official language alongside Fijian and Fiji Hindi (widely used in government, education, media, and commerce)
dialect_description: Fijian English (Fiji English) is a distinctive regional variety shaped by contact between Indigenous Fijian, Fiji Hindi, and British/Australian English. It serves as a major lingua franca across the island nation.
unique_vocabulary: bula (universal greeting used in local English)

phonetic_features.description: Dropping post-vocalic /r/ sounds in standard speech, heavily influenced by British and Australian models.
Pronouncing dental fricatives /θ/ and /ð/ as dental stops [t] and [d] in casual registers.
Exhibiting a syllable-timed rhythm influenced by Austronesian and Indo-Aryan speech patterns.

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 70-80% (widely spoken as a second or primary language across ethnic groups)

english_status: Official language (used in parliament, administration, law, and formal education)
dialect_description: Solomon Islands English is heavily influenced by Pijin (an English-based creole spoken as a lingua franca by over 90% of the population). Standard English is used in formal domains, while local speech features Oceanic phonology and creole grammar patterns.
unique_vocabulary: wantok (person from the same language group / close friend)
motu (food cooked in an underground stone oven)
luva (leave or abandon, borrowed from Pijin)

phonetic_features.description: Simplifying complex English vowel contrasts into a basic 5-vowel Oceanic system (a, e, i, o, u).
Replacing dental fricatives /θ/ and /ð/ with dental plosives [t] and [d].
Omitting final consonants in complex blends.

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 20-30% (Standard English in formal sectors, Pijin widely spoken)

english_status: Official language alongside Bislama and French (widely used in formal education, law, and international commerce)
dialect_description: Vanuatu English is heavily influenced by Bislama (an English-based creole and national language spoken by nearly the entire population) as well as French and local Austronesian languages, resulting in unique speech rhythms and simplified phonology.
unique_vocabulary: bislama (national creole language name used in daily English)
nakamal (traditional meeting place for drinking kava)
wantok (kin, friend, or person sharing the same language)

phonetic_features.description: Aligning complex English diphthongs and vowels onto a basic 5-vowel system (a, e, i, o, u) under Bislama influence.
Substituting dental fricatives /θ/ and /ð/ with dental plosives [t] and [d].
Simplifying complex word-final consonant blends.

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 25-35% (used in education, administration, alongside Bislama)

english_status: Official language alongside Setswana (widely used in government, business, secondary and higher education, and judiciary)
dialect_description: Botswana English is shaped by British English norms and heavily influenced by Setswana (Bantu) phonology, sentence structure, and cultural expressions. It features clear syllable-timed cadence and local idiom adaptations.
unique_vocabulary: kgotla (traditional community council or meeting place)
dumela (universal greeting adapted into local English dialogue)

phonetic_features.description: Omitting post-vocalic /r/ sounds, reflecting British colonial educational traditions.
Adopting the syllable-timed rhythmic structure of Setswana in English speech.
phonetic_features.examples: even syllable emphasis in formal speech

phonetic_features.description: Merging complex English diphthongs into monophthongal vowels influenced by Bantu phonology.

fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 40-50% (used in business, government, and higher education alongside Setswana)

english_status: Official language (constitutionally prescribed for the National Assembly, official documents, and formal education)
fluent_speakers_percentage: approx. 70-80% (widely used in business, administration, higher education, and media alongside Mauritian Creole and French)
dialect_description: Mauritian English is heavily influenced by British English standards due to historical administrative ties, while existing in a multilingual environment dominated by Mauritian Creole (Morisyen) and French in daily life.
unique_vocabulary: creole (primary lingua franca used interchangeably in daily life)
morisyen (local name for the Mauritian Creole language)
sugarcane (historically central to local economy and vocabulary)
baz (colloquial term for hangout spot or place)
ti-carré (small public square or open space)

phonetic_features.description: Dropping post-vocalic /r/, reflecting standard British educational norms.
Melodic intonation contours and speech rhythm shaped by Mauritian Creole phonology.
phonetic_features.examples: sentence stress shifts in casual speech

phonetic_features.description: Slight adaptations of vowel length under the influence of neighboring Romance and Bantu-derived creole sounds.
